title: Questions: What Information Is Missing?
description: Learn common Hawaiian question words and the yes/no particle anei through complete source-checked sentences.

sourceReview.notes: Source check, not educator review. Source spellings are normalized to Unicode ʻokina and NFC. Judd is not used to authorize any live form.

activities.instruction: Start with a question asking what something is.
activities.prompt: Notice what information the speaker is requesting.
activities.support: The whole phrase he aha functions together here.
activities.patternIntro: aha asks for missing information about what something is or what happened.
activities.languageNote: Do not reduce aha to a single fixed English word; its role depends on the whole question.

activities.instruction: Now ask for location.
activities.prompt: Track what kind of answer would satisfy the question.
activities.support: hea asks where or which, depending on structure.
activities.patternIntro: Here, ma hea asks for location.
activities.languageNote: The question word tells you what type of information the listener must supply.

activities.instruction: Ask who.
activities.prompt: The sentence is asking for a person or identity.
activities.support: wai is the interrogative for who.
activities.patternIntro: wai asks for a person's identity.
activities.languageNote: Recognizing wai immediately narrows the expected answer to a person or identity.

activities.instruction: Compare future and past 'when'.
activities.prompt: Hawaiian distinguishes these two question forms.
activities.support: āhea looks forward; ināhea asks about past time.
activities.sentence: Āhea ʻoe e hele mai ai?
activities.patternIntro: āhea asks when something will happen.
activities.languageNote: Later you will contrast this with ināhea for past-time questions.

activities.instruction: Now look backward in time.
activities.support: ināhea asks when something happened in the past.
activities.sentence: Ināhea ʻoe i hele mai ai?
activities.patternIntro: ināhea asks for a past time.
activities.languageNote: The question word itself helps establish the time orientation.

activities.instruction: Ask how many or how much.
activities.prompt: Think about the kind of answer expected.
activities.support: ʻehia asks for a quantity.
activities.languageNote: The listener should expect to answer with a quantity.

activities.instruction: See a yes/no question marker.
activities.prompt: Unlike a question word, anei makes the whole statement a yes/no question.
activities.support: This source sentence asks whether the listener has seen Keola.
activities.sentence: Ua ʻike anei ʻoe i Keola?
activities.patternIntro: anei marks a yes/no question without replacing a noun.

parts.label: Action
parts.note: saw / have seen in this context

activities.languageNote: The expected response is yes/no or equivalent confirmation, not a missing person/place/quantity.
